hints: Focus on what the first propagation step really does, a chlorine radical removes an H to leave a carbon radical behind.
Draw out pentane as $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and label the carbons 1 to 5 from left to right.
Check for symmetry by pairing carbons from opposite ends, then count how many unique positions can lose an H to give a different radical.
walkthrough:
**Recall what first propagation means**

Think of it simply as $\text{Cl} \bullet$ stealing one H from the alkane.

General equation:
$$\text{R-H} + \text{Cl}\bullet \rightarrow \text{R}\bullet + \text{HCl}$$

**Draw pentane and look for different H environments**

Pentane is a straight chain:
$$\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$$
Label the carbons 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 from left to right. Carbon 1 matches carbon 5, and carbon 2 matches carbon 4, because the molecule is symmetrical.

**Count the unique radicals**

Removing an H from C1 (same as C5) gives a primary radical $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\bullet$.

Removing an H from C2 (same as C4) gives a secondary radical $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}\bullet\text{CH}_3$.

Removing an H from C3 gives a different secondary radical $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}\bullet\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. That is 3 different first propagation steps in total.

options.A: 2 is too few. It correctly spots primary and secondary H atoms, but misses that there are two different secondary positions in pentane, at C2 and at C3.
options.B: 3 is correct. Pentane has three distinct H environments: on C1/C5, on C2/C4, and on C3, so $\text{Cl}\bullet$ can form three different pentyl radicals and three different $\text{R-H} + \text{Cl}\bullet \rightarrow \text{R}\bullet + \text{HCl}$ equations.
options.C: 4 is incorrect. It may come from counting C1, C2, C3, C4 as different and forgetting that C4 is identical to C2 by symmetry, and C5 is identical to C1.
options.D: 5 is incorrect. It counts all five carbons as different and ignores symmetry completely. In a straight chain, opposite ends are equivalent.
